item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Absolutely stunning.
The medium of an orientation to fade into the pamphlet was well done in my eyes as a means to get into the real meat of the tale. The meticulous planning and detailing in this article is highly evident and manages to craft a highly intricate story that comes off as realistic and intriguing. Many I have noticed have complained that the military action is unrealistic in its large scale for a secret organization, but I actually found this as one of the strongest points: I think it effectively highlights the sheer raw power wielded by the Foundation and how an entire world-wide conflict can be waged and yet completely covered up by the omnipotent powers of the Foundation. The Manifesto and Speech are powerful and characterize the CI and their strategy/ ideology moving foreword beautifully. Overall, this satisfied the history geek in me and is now part of my head-cannon.

+1

Excellent, although I have one small nitpick.

The idea of "large troop movements" between two secret organizations seems far too conspicuous. I'd rather that the war have been fought in a secret manner with heavy use of small unit tactics, and both sides basically waging a guerrilla war against each other. "Battles" can be what we'd call commando raids and large-scale firefights between groups of up to company size.

Basically, little to none of what we'd call "conventional warfare" and more of unconventional warfare.

Otherwise, as a fellow history major, military history nerd and another user interested in the CI, I adore your interpretation. Here is your +1.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Gaaaaah. I finally finished reading this, and… I'm going to have an unpopular opinion, because I really didn't like it.

I kept finding myself impressed by the amount of detail and work that was put into this. Effort-wise, it's brilliant. The scope and complexity are excellent. It was ballsy to go this far.

But then I'd realize that all those details were cliched, and the writing itself is extremely repetitive and bloated. The CI guys all have stereotypical elements — I mean, "Damien", seriously? One of the eeeevil O5s was a "Count"? "Count Fredericks" just makes me lol. And of course the other one is a nasty General. "Triad" is cribbed from a real-life crime organization.

And then there's the fact that reading most of this feels like a generic alternate history novel. No. Rather, the excessively detailed Wikipedia plot summary of an alternate history novel. You have an outright war between the Foundation and the Insurgency, …and it's pretty much just like any other war? My favorite 'anomalous' detail was the tornado thing, which is randomly caused by MC&D because lol we need a cameo (seriously, that was a good idea, but why MC&D?). Why even write this in the SCP universe if you're not going to use SCPs? Let alone write it about an organization conceptually based on using rather than containing SCPs. So much wasted potential.

The Related Original Documents are… well, they're alright. Conceptually, they're pretty nice, and they have a few good lines — "Let us wage a war of fleas" is particularly good. But they're still over-written and excessively meandering (sort of like this post of mine!) — and for that matter, why are both documents like this, and not just one of 'em? Is it a Villain Trait or something?

And the original issue I called out remains, regarding the framing device.

By far the coolest part of this is the moniker "Slate Thunder". As for the rest… The scope and scale and amount and complexity of detail work are good traits, as is the realism in presentation (if not in detail). And the documents are decent. I suspect those traits are enough for most people, especially because no one's actually picked out many details to call good despite the sheer weight of detail here (the sheer weight of detail is most often referenced as the thing that makes it good, actually).

But that's not enough for me, so I'm downvoting.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I would love to see this same sequence of events as presented by an Insurgent.

Something for me to put on my to-do list, I suppose, unless somebody beats me to it.

I was aiming for the history pamphlet to read as victor-biased, not because of an inherent sense of superiority on the in-universe author (Professor Greg Lewis), but because Lewis is a product of the Foundation's institutional biases. If anything, I suspect that the O5 Council would view Lewis' account of the history as presented in the pamphlet as being as close to unbiased as they could politically allow. Thus, Lewis (like any good intelligence analyst) has the mission of "speaking (in this case unpopular) truth to power", but cannot frame that truth in truly unbiased terms.

In short, while the intended nuance is more subtly complicated than "history by the victors" (though that is definitely a good simple rendering of it), I'm glad I managed to at least pull that off.

I know I've taken some criticism by people for handling the tone of this piece (in particular of the narrator giving the briefing), which is fine, but I generally chose (and choose) my words very carefully to give subtlety and nuance to the writing in respect to what's going on at levels beyond the surface. It is unfortunate that my writing has been unsuccessful in conveying that to certain readers.

I never thought much of the Chaos Insurgency. They just never seemed as interesting as other GoIs. But you've fleshed them out so completly and believably that they are my new favorites, for at least the next ten minutes.

I got a strong impression of "history by the victors". Everything the Triad did is slanted as either nefarious, traitorous, or stupid; while even the worst abuses and blunders by the Foundation are spun as regrettable necessities or the fault of even more traitors. I would love to see this same sequence of events as presented by an Insurgent.

The tragic, yet hopeful, story of how good men of strong moral fiber refused to stand idle while a self-apointed oligarchy abused the men and women who worked to protect the world from horrors unendurable. How the "Opressors Council" refused to allow even the idea of dissent, and ultimately left the peace-loving heros no choice but armed rebellion.

item.title: Oh wait, I wasn't the only one with this problem?
item.content:encoded:
I thought I was the only one who had problems with this tale.

It reads so boring that by paragraph 4 I scrolled up, downvoted, skimmed the rest for anything that made up for the borefest and found nothing. If you want to outline a headcanon you can do that by cutting out the introductory narrative. The real meat is the tabbed stuff. The rest is just fleshy tumors growing off. At first I thought this was because I was in a bad mood and at work, so my brain didn't operate correctly in analyzing the narrative. Now that I'm home and marginally in a better mood I realize that, no, my original reading was correct and this reads like some boring textbook.

There are no characters. Just faceless cardboard cutouts of people, a blank white frame around a picture. Except the picture is so small and the frame is much too large. This, paired with a narrator that has absolutely no weight in his words (no twinges of word play, no personality, the barest attempt at humor (doesn't work), no different ways to say things, colloquialisms, nothing) makes it a chore to read and by the time I got to the 'real' tale, I wanted nothing to do with it at all.
